subject: english
text:
The Great Pyramid of Khufu was finished about 4,500 years ago, and it remained the tallest human-made structure on Earth for nearly four thousand years. How such a monument was built has fascinated people for centuries.

In the fifth century BC, a Greek traveller named Herodotus visited Egypt and wrote that 100,000 people were forced to haul stones for twenty years. He arrived about two thousand years after the pyramid was finished, and he repeated what local guides told him. For this reason, many modern scholars treat his account with caution. Still, his story shaped books and films for a very long time.

In the 1990s, archaeologists uncovered a large settlement and cemeteries close to the Giza pyramids. They found bakeries, breweries and sleeping halls, together with thousands of animal bones, which suggest the builders ate plenty of beef. The workers' tombs were built beside the king's own monument, an honour that was not normally given to slaves. Some tombs even show the names of work crews, such as "Friends of Khufu".

Experts now estimate that the workforce was perhaps 20,000 to 30,000 people, organised into rotating crews. Some may have been farmers who joined the project during the Nile flood, when their fields were underwater. Others were skilled stonecutters. This does not mean the work was easy, because skeletons show injuries from heavy lifting. However, the evidence suggests that the pyramid was a national project rather than a prison sentence. Today, researchers keep digging, so our picture of the pyramid builders may keep changing as new clues are found.

subject: english
text:
In April 1770, the Endeavour anchored in Botany Bay on the east coast of Australia. Two very different kinds of record describe what happened next, and historians learn the most by reading both.

The ship's records are written down. Lieutenant James Cook and the botanist Joseph Banks kept detailed journals about the coast, the weather, the plants and the animals they saw. Banks collected so many new plants that the bay was later named Botany Bay. In these journals, the voyage is often described as a "discovery", because the writers were describing places that were new to Europeans.

The other records are spoken. For the Gweagal people of Kamay, the bay was not a new place. It was Country that had been known, named and cared for for tens of thousands of years. Oral histories, which are passed from one generation to the next, preserve memories of the ship's arrival. Many First Nations people today point out that the word "discovery" leaves out those who already lived here.

Journals have the advantage of recording dates, measurements and daily events in the writers' own words. Oral histories have the advantage of carrying the viewpoint of the local people and have been kept alive for generations through careful teaching. Neither source tells the whole story alone. By placing them side by side, historians can see that one event can look very different depending on who is telling it.

Because of this, many museums now display journals and oral histories together. In this way, visitors can think about more than one point of view.

text:
Long before telescopes, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples were studying the sky. Their observations were not just for wonder. The sky was a tool for living well on the land and sea.

In some Aboriginal communities, the dark shape of the Emu in the Sky tells people when to collect emu eggs. When the emu appears to be running along the horizon in the evening, the egg-laying season is starting. Because the emu is made from dark patches of the Milky Way, not from bright stars, it can be seen best on clear, moonless nights away from city lights.

In the Torres Strait, the Tagai constellation shows a fisherman standing in his canoe. Its position in the sky helps people know the seasons, including when to plant gardens and when to fish. Because the islands are surrounded by sea, careful knowledge of the stars also helped people navigate between islands.

In northern Australia, some Yolngu stories link the Moon to the tides. People noticed that the tides rise and fall in time with the Moon, and the stories carry that knowledge. Scientists today agree that the Moon's gravity causes tides.

Each nation has its own sky stories, and each story belongs to its own people. Knowledge was shared in song, dance and ceremony, so it could be remembered without books. When we read about this knowledge, it is important to show respect, and to remember that these are living cultures, not just history. Learning about it can change how we look at the night sky.

text:
Many early castles in Europe were not built from stone. Around 1066, soldiers could raise a wooden tower on a mound of earth fairly quickly. These early castles were quick to build, but wood had a problem. It rotted over time, and attackers could set it on fire.

For this reason, lords began to rebuild their castles in stone. A stone keep, or main tower, could last for hundreds of years. However, the new walls created a new challenge. Attackers learned to dig tunnels under the corners of square towers, which weakened them until they fell. To solve this, builders began making towers round. A round tower has no sharp corner to dig under, and its curved surface is better at turning aside stones thrown by war machines.

Defenders also invented clever features. Narrow windows allowed archers to shoot while staying safe. Overhanging platforms let guards drop stones on attackers who came too close. A deep moat made it difficult to dig tunnels or place ladders against the walls.

In the fifteenth century, cannons using gunpowder changed everything. Cannons could batter even thick stone walls. A tall wall, once a strength, now made a bigger target. Over time, lords decided that castles were not worth the expense. Many moved into comfortable manor houses with large windows and gardens. Castles became ruins, museums or tourist attractions, remembered as clever solutions to old problems. Visitors who walk through them today can still spot the moats, narrow windows and round towers. Each one tells a small story about how people solved problems with the tools they had.

subject: english
text:
People often use the words weather and climate as if they mean the same thing, but they do not. Weather is what is happening outside today: sunny, windy or wet. Climate is the pattern of weather in a place measured over many years. Sydney might have a rainy week in summer, but its climate is still warm and mostly mild.

Climate depends on many causes. One is distance from the sea. Water heats up and cools down slowly, so places on the coast usually have gentler temperatures than places far inland. Another cause is mountains.

Imagine wet air blowing in from the ocean towards a mountain range. The wind is forced upwards along the slope. As it rises, the air cools, and the water vapour in it condenses into clouds. The clouds release rain or snow on the side of the mountain facing the wind. By the time the air crosses the top and sinks down the other side, most of its water is gone. The air becomes warmer and drier, so the far side of the mountain receives little rain. Scientists call this a rain shadow.

Australia's Great Dividing Range is a good example. Moist winds from the Pacific Ocean drop rain on the coast side, which is why many eastern coastal areas are green. Inland on the western side, the land becomes much drier, and farmers there must plan carefully for dry spells.

Understanding climate helps people decide where to build towns, grow crops and store water. Weather forecasts help us plan the week, but climate helps us plan for the years ahead.

text:
In 79 AD, Mount Vesuvius in Italy erupted and buried the Roman town of Pompeii under ash and pumice. Surprisingly, many people now live around that same volcano. Hundreds of thousands live in the zone that scientists consider the most at risk. Why would anyone choose to live there?

One reason is the soil. When ash and lava break down, they release minerals that plants need. Vineyards, olive groves and vegetable farms flourish on the slopes of Vesuvius, and the region produces some of Italy's finest food. Another reason is that the ruins of Pompeii, which were preserved by the ash, now attract millions of visitors each year, which provides jobs.

Volcanoes can also provide energy. In Iceland, hot rock beneath the ground heats water that is piped to homes and greenhouses. This geothermal energy is clean and cheap, so most Icelandic homes are warmed without burning fuel.

Of course, living near a volcano needs careful planning. Scientists monitor the volcano with instruments that measure tiny earthquakes, changes in the ground and gases. If signs suggest an eruption, authorities have plans to move people to safety. Because of this monitoring, an eruption is less likely to take people by surprise.

Overall, living near a volcano is a trade-off. People accept some risk in return for fertile land, work and energy. With good science and planning, many communities believe the benefits are worth it. The people of Vesuvius show that, with respect for nature, communities can live alongside even powerful volcanoes. Scientists will keep studying them closely.

text:
Theo sat on the bench with his chin in his hands. Every Saturday it was the same. Coach Pham named the starting players, and every Saturday, Theo's name was not on the list. He was the substitute.

"It isn't fair," he muttered. He watched his best friend, Ravi, run onto the field wearing the number nine shirt that Theo wanted. Part of him hoped that Ravi would miss an easy shot. As soon as the thought arrived, he felt uncomfortable, as if he had swallowed something sour.

Ravi did not miss. He scored twice before half-time, and Theo clapped, though his hands felt heavy. During the break, Coach Pham sat down beside him. "Do you know why I like having you on the bench?" she asked. Theo shook his head. "Because you watch the game. Yesterday you told me that the other team's left side is slow. That tip is why we are winning."

Theo had not thought of it that way. In the second half he called out helpful messages from the sideline, and when a defender was injured near the end, the coach sent him on. He wasn't brilliant, but he stayed calm and passed the ball quickly. The final whistle blew with the score at 3-1.

Walking home, Ravi patted him on the back. "Thanks for the tip," he said. Theo smiled. He still wanted the number nine shirt, but he no longer felt sour. He realised that being part of a team meant helping everyone win, not only himself.

subject: english
text:
Nadia and her cousin Sam were on a school camp hike along a ridge in the bush. The group had been walking for two hours when a thick fog rolled in. In a few minutes, they could not see the leader ahead, or the trees ten steps away.

Nadia had stopped to tie her shoelace, and when she stood, the others had disappeared into the white. "Hello?" she called. Only the dripping of leaves answered. Sam, who had been walking behind her, caught up. His eyes were wide.

"Which way did they go?" he asked. "Let's run. We can catch up."

Nadia remembered what Ms Lee had told them that morning. If you lose the group, stop, think and stay together. She took a long breath. "Running might take us the wrong way," she said. "Let's work out what we know." They stood close together, shouted as loudly as they could, and then listened. "Let's stay here and keep listening," said Nadia.

They waited side by side and called out every few seconds. Between calls, they listened hard while the cold fog pressed around them and their hearts thumped. After a few minutes, they heard a whistle, then voices. Ms Lee had stopped the group when she counted heads and had been blowing her whistle to guide them back.

"Well done for staying calm," she said. Nadia smiled. The fog had not changed, but she felt as clear as the morning. Panic would have made them lose their way, while a calm plan had found it.

text:
During the Olympic Games, television screens fill with Olympic athletes standing on podiums with medals around their necks. What viewers rarely see is everything that happened before that moment.

Many Olympic athletes begin training when they are young and keep going for many years. They practise nearly every day, often before school or work. A swimmer might spend hours in the pool, then more hours lifting weights and stretching. Coaches watch closely and suggest small changes, such as a different arm movement or a slightly earlier start. Over months, these tiny improvements can add up to a faster time.

Rest matters just as much as effort. Athletes who train without enough sleep or recovery can become tired or injured. For this reason, many follow a careful routine that includes healthy meals, plenty of sleep and days off. Some also learn to manage nerves by breathing slowly or picturing a good performance in their minds.

Setbacks are common. An athlete may miss a team by a fraction of a second, or an injury may force a long break from competing. Many describe these times as the hardest part of their careers. Yet a lot of them say the disappointment taught them patience and determination.

Athletes also rely on other people. Families drive them to practice, teammates push them to improve, and volunteers help to run events. Only a few athletes in each event win a medal, but thousands take part, and many are proud simply to have reached the Games. The story behind a medal is rarely about one person or one lucky day. It is about steady work, support and the courage to keep trying.

subject: english
text:
On a warm night, a female sea turtle drags herself slowly up a sandy beach. She is huge compared with the hatchlings that will later crawl out of her nest, and the journey from the water has left her tired. Using her back flippers, she digs a deep hole and lays around a hundred soft, round eggs. Then she covers the nest with sand and returns to the sea. Her work is finished, and the nest is left to the warm sand.

About two months later, the eggs begin to hatch. The baby turtles, called hatchlings, are smaller than a human hand. They wait underground until the sand cools at night, then burst out together. Scientists believe that emerging at night helps hatchlings avoid hot sand and some daytime predators such as gulls.

The hatchlings must now reach the water. They usually move towards the lowest, brightest horizon, which on a natural beach is the open sea, because land is darker and often has dunes or trees. However, bright lights from roads, hotels and houses can confuse them. Instead of heading to the ocean, some crawl towards the lights and become lost or exhausted. In some places, communities now switch off beach lights during hatching season or use special lamps that are easier on turtles.

Even a hatchling that reaches the water faces many dangers. Crabs, fish and seabirds eat the young turtles, and only a small number survive to adulthood. Those that do may live for many decades. Some females are thought to return to lay their own eggs on or near the beach where they hatched, even after travelling thousands of kilometres.

People can help sea turtles in simple ways. Picking up rubbish from beaches, keeping lights low on turtle beaches at night and giving nests space all make a difference. A small action on land can protect an animal whose life begins in the sand and continues across the ocean.

subject: english
text:
For seventy-six years, schoolchildren learned that the Solar System had nine planets. Pluto was found in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh, a young American astronomer, and it was welcomed as the ninth planet. Yet from the start it was odd. It is smaller than Earth's Moon, and its orbit is stretched and tilted, so that for part of each journey around the Sun it is actually closer to the Sun than Neptune.

In the 1990s, astronomers began to find other icy bodies beyond Neptune, in a region now called the Kuiper Belt. Then, in 2005, a team announced the discovery of Eris, an object that first appeared to be larger than Pluto and was later found to be slightly smaller but heavier. If Pluto was a planet, many people asked, was Eris one too? And what about the many others that might still be waiting to be found?

In 2006, members of the International Astronomical Union voted on a definition. To be a planet, an object must orbit the Sun, be round because of its own gravity, and have cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit of other large objects. Pluto meets the first two rules, but it shares its orbital zone with many other icy bodies, so it failed the third. It was placed in a new group called dwarf planets.

The decision upset many people, and some scientists still disagree with it. Yet it did not change Pluto itself. In 2015, the New Horizons spacecraft flew past and sent back pictures of mountains of water ice and a large, heart-shaped plain. Whatever we call it, Pluto turned out to be a fascinating world. The story also shows that science is willing to change its categories when the evidence changes.

text:
Rome at its height was home to about a million people, and every one of them needed water. Wells and the Tiber River could not supply enough, so Roman engineers built aqueducts, channels that carried fresh water from springs and rivers many kilometres away. The city eventually received water from about eleven of them.

The Romans did have simple hand-worked pumps, but no machine of their time could push a whole river's worth of water over long distances. Instead, they used gravity. An aqueduct was built to slope very gently downhill along its whole length, dropping by only a small amount for every hundred metres. If the slope was too steep, the water would race along and wear away the channel. If it was too shallow, the water would barely move. Surveyors had to measure the slope with simple tools, and the accuracy of their work still impresses engineers today.

Much of an aqueduct actually ran underground, where it was protected from damage and kept the water cooler and cleaner. The famous stone arches appeared only where the channel had to cross a valley while staying at the right height. One of these, the Pont du Gard in southern France, still stands, almost fifty metres tall.

Aqueducts supplied public fountains, bathhouses and, for the wealthy, private homes. They were a source of pride, and officials were appointed to keep them in repair. Yet they also depended on constant care. When Rome's empire weakened in later centuries, enemies cut some of the channels, and with no money for repairs, many fell into ruin. This shows that clever engineering alone cannot last without people willing to maintain it.

text:
Electric cars have no exhaust pipe, and they make no smoke as they drive, which makes them seem like a perfect solution to pollution. The truth is more complicated, and sensible people weigh several trade-offs.

First, consider the benefits. An electric motor wastes far less energy than a petrol engine, which turns much of its fuel into heat. Electric cars are also quieter, and they cut pollution in busy streets, which is good for people's lungs. Over its whole life, including the energy used to build it, an electric car usually produces less carbon dioxide than a similar petrol car, and the gap grows as electricity networks use more wind, solar and hydro power.

Now consider the costs. A large battery needs metals such as lithium, nickel and cobalt, and mining them can damage land and water if it is not carefully managed. Making a battery also uses a lot of energy, so a new electric car begins its life with a larger carbon footprint than a similar petrol car. It takes time on the road to pay back that difference. Charging can also be a problem for people who live in apartments without a private parking space, and long trips need fast chargers along the way.

Finally, the picture is changing. Batteries are being recycled so that their metals can be used again, and makers are developing designs that use less cobalt. Cities are adding more public chargers each year.

An electric car is therefore not magic, but neither is it a trick. For most drivers, it is one useful tool among several, alongside trains, buses, bikes and walking.

subject: english
text:
Along tropical coasts, where many plants would die in salty mud, mangrove trees thrive. They grow in the zone between land and sea, and their tangled roots rise out of the water like the legs of a spider. These roots solve two problems at once. Because the mud has little oxygen, many mangrove species send up roots that stick out of the ground and take in air. Other roots grow down and spread wide, holding the tree upright in soft, shifting soil. Some mangroves can also remove salt from the water they take up, and some push it out through their leaves.

The roots do much more than keep the trees alive. Fish, crabs and prawns shelter among them, and for many ocean species, mangroves serve as a nursery where young animals grow up safely before heading out to the open water. Birds nest in the branches above. The roots also slow the movement of water, which lets mud and sand settle, so the shoreline is held in place rather than washed away.

Mangroves can also protect people. Studies suggest that thick belts of mangroves reduce the height and force of waves, which helps shield villages from storms, though they cannot stop the largest surges. They also store large amounts of carbon in their wood and in the soil beneath them, which helps to slow climate change.

Despite all these benefits, mangroves have been cleared in many places for shrimp farms, ports and building. Scientists estimate that the world has lost a large share of its mangrove forests over the past fifty years, but many countries are now protecting what remains and planting new trees along coasts.

subject: english
text:
When the storm knocked out the power, the whole street fell silent. Maya, who had been halfway through a video game, stared at the dead screen and groaned. In the kitchen, her grandmother, Nana Rosa, was already lighting candles as calmly as if this happened every week. Even the fridge had stopped humming, and the quiet felt strange.

"Come and sit," said Nana Rosa. "We have no electricity, but we have plenty of time." Maya rolled her eyes and sat at the table with her arms folded. Outside, the wind rattled the shutters.

Nana Rosa pulled out a battered tin of buttons. "Every button here is a story," she said, holding up a tiny silver one. "This was from the coat I wore the day I arrived in this country. I was eleven, and I did not speak a word of English." Maya looked up. She had never heard this before. Her grandmother had always seemed to belong to the house, like the old clock in the hall.

"Weren't you scared?" Maya asked.

"Terrified," said Nana Rosa. "But a girl next door gave me a sandwich and pointed at the playground. That was how I learned my first word. She said, 'Friend.'" Her eyes were bright in the candlelight.

For an hour Maya sorted through the buttons and listened. By the time the lights flickered back on, she hardly noticed. When her phone buzzed with a message from her friends, she turned it face down on the table. "Tell me about the red one," she said.
